clean-core.title: Decouple Extensions from Standard (SAP Learning, clean core extensibility)
clean-core.notes: This SAP Learning unit treats clean core extensibility as one dimension of keeping an SAP S/4HANA system clean, summed up by the idea of keeping extensions clean so that they stay separate from SAP code, upgrades run smoothly and the system remains maintainable. It advises avoiding extensions where standard features or configuration already meet the need, governing approvals with documented reasons and value, and making sure extensions never break upgrades and upgrades never break extensions. Extensions come in on-stack forms created inside S/4HANA Cloud (key user and developer extensions) and side-by-side forms built on SAP Business Technology Platform. They may use only released objects such as released public APIs, BAdIs and RAP business object extension points, never unreleased ones; the ABAP Cloud model enforces this through syntax checks. A three-tier model ranks approaches: tier 1 uses only ABAP Cloud and the cloud extensibility model and is mandatory for Public Edition, tier 2 wraps unreleased objects in released ones for Private Edition and on-premise systems, and tier 3 covers classical extensions, which are discouraged because they are likely to disrupt upgrades. The SAP Application Extension Methodology helps assess use cases and choose a target solution.

project-management-office.title: Project management office (Wikipedia)
project-management-office.notes: A project management office is a group or department inside a business, agency or enterprise that sets and maintains project management standards, aiming to standardize execution and gain efficiency from repeated practice. It serves as the source of documentation, guidance and metrics, often building on PRINCE2 or the PMBOK guide. Typical functions include defining methodology, facilitating or owning portfolio management, monitoring active projects and portfolios, and reporting progress to top management so they can decide which projects to continue or cancel. The article distinguishes three control levels: supportive (consultative), controlling (requires compliance) and directive (takes over project management). It lists types such as the enterprise PMO, which aligns projects with strategy, has the broadest remit and usually reports to the CEO or an equivalent role; the divisional PMO for one business unit; the project PMO that exists for a single large project or program; and the project management center of excellence.  A PricewaterhouseCoopers survey of 1,524 organizations cited in the text names an established PMO among the top three drivers of successful delivery, though researchers argue many PMO practices lack evidence and PMOs cannot be sorted into fixed types.

manufacturing-execution-system.title: Manufacturing execution system (Wikipedia)
manufacturing-execution-system.notes: Manufacturing execution systems are computerized systems that track and document how raw materials become finished goods, giving decision makers a view of current plant-floor conditions and producing an as-built record of process, data and outcomes. That record is especially valuable in regulated industries such as food and pharmaceuticals. Typical functions are product definition management (master data, bills of material, recipes), resource management, scheduling of work orders from ERP or planning systems, dispatching to work centers, execution reporting, data collection, performance analysis such as overall equipment effectiveness, and track and trace of lots and orders. Cited benefits include less waste, rework and scrap, more accurate cost capture, less downtime, paperless workflows and lower inventory. The MESA association defined 11 functions, and the ANSI/ISA-95 standard places MES at Level 3, between ERP at Level 4 and process control at Levels 0 to 2; Part 3 splits Level 3 into production, quality, logistics and maintenance. MES exchanges work instructions and set points with SCADA, PLC and DCS systems, often via OPC-UA, and data with ERP via B2MML.

copilot-analytics.title: Introduction to Copilot Analytics (Microsoft Learn)
copilot-analytics.notes: Microsoft Copilot Analytics is a set of tools in Microsoft 365 and Viva Insights that shows organizations how employees use Copilot and what impact it has, so they can decide how to roll it out and improve productivity. It has six areas: the readiness and adoption reports in the Microsoft 365 admin center, the Microsoft Copilot Dashboard for leaders and managers, an Agent Dashboard, a Consumption Dashboard that tracks credit use against limits, ready-made Copilot Analytics reports, and Advanced Reporting with Power BI templates and more than 100 Copilot metrics. Every employee with a Copilot license is automatically given a Viva Insights service plan and becomes part of the measured population; agents with Entra ID are not measured. The Copilot Dashboard needs a Microsoft 365 or Office 365 business or enterprise subscription with Exchange Online, and data typically appears within seven days of license assignment. The Agent Dashboard requires at least 50 Copilot licenses. Advanced Reporting is limited to users with the Insights Analyst role and supports uploading organizational or business outcome data to relate usage to results such as ticket resolution time or retention.

smartart.title: Create a SmartArt graphic in PowerPoint (Microsoft Support)
smartart.notes: This Microsoft Support how-to describes SmartArt as a way to add visual impact to plain text and bullet lists by turning them into diagrams chosen from a gallery of layouts. To create one from existing text, you select the text, use the Home tab command for converting to a SmartArt graphic, and then pick the layout you prefer. The article also explains how to use layouts that include picture placeholders: choose a layout from the Picture category in the SmartArt gallery, then click the picture icon to browse for an image and insert it. The page states that it applies to PowerPoint for Microsoft 365 and to PowerPoint 2024, 2021, 2019 and 2016. It is deliberately short and does not cover converting a SmartArt graphic back into plain text or shapes; for that and for other SmartArt details it points readers to a separate, more general article on SmartArt graphics. It is a useful reference for the basic text-to-diagram workflow in PowerPoint rather than a full description of every Office application that supports the feature.

operational-technology.title: Operational technology (Wikipedia)
operational-technology.notes: Operational technology is hardware and software that detects or causes change by directly monitoring and controlling industrial equipment, assets, processes and events, as distinct from information technology; the article jokingly calls it IT in the non-carpeted areas. OT environments include industrial control systems such as SCADA, distributed control systems, remote terminal units and programmable logic controllers, and also IoT and industrial IoT devices and building automation. These systems regulate values such as temperature, pressure and flow and need real-time or near-real-time processing with high reliability. They use specialized protocols such as Modbus, DNP3, Profibus, BACnet and OPC-UA, and priorities differ from IT: OT stresses availability and real-time control, while IT centers on confidentiality, integrity and availability. Gartner introduced the term in 2006, first for power utility control systems. Security was long based on isolation and obscurity; since at least 2005 OT has been connected to IT systems, which created risks illustrated by Stuxnet, including weak segmentation, plaintext protocols and legacy devices without authentication. The page recommends layered defenses, continuous anomaly monitoring and the ISA/IEC 62443 series,.

critical-path-method.title: Critical path method (Wikipedia)
critical-path-method.notes: The critical path method is a scheduling algorithm for a set of project activities. From a list of activities, their durations, dependencies and milestones, it finds the longest chain of dependent activities, which sets the shortest possible project duration, and it computes earliest and latest start and finish times. Activities on the critical path have zero total float, so any slip delays the whole project, while others have slack. The article also defines critical path drag, near-critical paths and the effect of constraints. Managers use the results to prioritize work and shorten schedules by fast-tracking (more parallel work) or crashing (adding resources at extra cost). CPM was developed in the late 1950s by Morgan Walker of DuPont and James Kelley Jr. of Remington Rand, related to PERT, and was used in 1966 on the World Trade Center towers. It is applied in construction, aerospace, software, research and manufacturing. Extensions add resource leveling and the resource critical path. Limits include sensitivity to estimate errors, the need to keep monitoring because non-critical tasks can exceed their float and create a new critical path, and criticism of as-built critical path analysis in court.

gitflow.title: Gitflow Workflow (Atlassian Git Tutorial)
gitflow.notes: Gitflow is a Git branching model, popularized by Vincent Driessen, built on feature branches and several primary branches. The main branch holds the official release history, usually tagged with version numbers, while develop is the integration branch for finished features. Feature branches start from develop and merge back into it. When enough features are ready, a release branch forks from develop for stabilization work only, such as bug fixes and documentation, and is then merged into main with a tag and back into develop. Hotfix branches fork directly from main to patch production and are merged into both main and develop. The tutorial notes that Gitflow adds no new Git commands beyond the feature branch workflow, only roles for branches, and that a git-flow extension wraps the steps. It suits projects with scheduled release cycles, teams that want separate release and development phases, and code review through pull requests. Atlassian labels it a legacy workflow that has fallen out of favor against trunk-based development, because long-lived branches cause hard merges and drift, and it is harder to combine with continuous integration and delivery.

team-topologies.title: Team Topologies key concepts (teamtopologies.com)
team-topologies.notes: Team Topologies is an approach for designing organizations as a team of teams that can deliver value quickly, offering a pattern language and thinking model for matching team design to the target architecture and fast flow. It defines four fundamental team types: stream-aligned teams that own work end to end for a segment of the business domain, enabling teams that temporarily help others overcome obstacles and build skills, complicated-subsystem teams that handle components needing deep specialist expertise, and platform teams that provide an internal product to reduce complexity for stream-aligned teams. It also defines three interaction modes: collaboration (high bandwidth, defined period), X-as-a-Service (minimal interaction, clear boundaries) and facilitation (helping or mentoring). Supporting practices include managing cognitive load, the thinnest viable platform, flexible team boundaries and continuous adaptation. The page lists nine principles, such as focusing on flow, high trust, small safe changes and eliminating dependencies. It stresses that the approach is not a method for drawing an org chart, that no single part works alone, and that team relationships are snapshots that change over time.

fido-alliance.title: FIDO Alliance (Wikipedia)
fido-alliance.notes: The FIDO (Fast IDentity Online) Alliance is an open industry association based in Beaverton, Oregon, launched in February 2013 to reduce reliance on passwords. It targets two problems: strong authentication devices that do not interoperate, and the burden of managing many usernames and passwords. Its model is device-centric: a device registers a public key with a server, and to log in it signs a server challenge with a private key that a local gesture such as a fingerprint scan or button press unlocks, so authentication works over an insecure channel using public-key cryptography. Specifications include UAF, U2F as a second factor, and FIDO2, a joint project with the W3C made of WebAuthn and CTAP2. WebAuthn became a W3C Recommendation in March 2019. Authenticators can be hardware security keys, smartphones, TPMs, smart cards or NFC devices. Members include large technology, payment and government organizations such as Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Samsung, Intel, Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Yubico and NIST. The article does not discuss passkeys by name.

docker-hub.title: Docker Hub (Docker Docs)
docker-hub.notes: Docker Hub is a container image registry, described in Docker's documentation as the world's largest registry for storing, managing and sharing Docker images. It integrates with developer tools to support deployment and distribution of containerized applications and offers pre-built images and assets to speed up development. Listed features include unlimited public repositories, private repositories, webhooks for automating workflows, GitHub and Bitbucket integrations, concurrent and automated builds, and trusted content, meaning curated, high-quality, secure images. Users can work with it through the web interface, the Docker Hub API, an experimental CLI tool, and a Docker Hub MCP server for integrating AI agents. The documentation hub points to sections on a quickstart, the library with search, trusted content and mirrors, repositories, settings, organizations, usage and limits, and release notes. The navigation marks automated builds as deprecated. The page is part of Docker's official documentation and acts as an overview and entry point rather than a detailed reference for each feature.

freight-reconciliation.title: Reconcile freight in transportation management (Microsoft Learn)
freight-reconciliation.notes: In Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management, freight reconciliation, also called matching, compares system-generated freight bills, which carry estimated freight costs, with the actual invoices received from carriers. Differences are variances and are resolved with reconciliation reason codes that determine how amounts are posted in the general ledger. The flow is: the carrier rate engine calculates rates and a freight bill is created when a load is confirmed; the carrier invoice arrives electronically or on paper; invoices are matched to freight bills line by line or automatically; variances are handled; and the invoice is submitted for approval before the journal is posted. Setup includes enabling freight reconciliation in the transportation parameters, reconciliation reasons, billing groups, freight bill types that define matching criteria, and an audit master with minimum and maximum tolerances that block automatic reconciliation when differences are too large. Automatic matching sorts invoices by amount, largest first, and applies them until the freight bill is fully matched. The page advises matching negative-amount invoices manually and first, and recommends a match interval of at least 120 seconds when automatic matching is on.

factory-simulation.title: Discrete-event simulation (Wikipedia)
factory-simulation.notes: Discrete-event simulation models a system as a sequence of events in time, each marking a change of state at a specific instant, with the state assumed constant between events. The usual approach jumps the clock to the next event, which is faster than slicing time into small steps, and a pending event set, normally a time-ordered priority queue, holds scheduled events. Randomness comes from pseudorandom number generators, so runs can be repeated exactly; early output may be misleading until steady state is reached, results are averaged over replications with confidence intervals, and a stopping rule must be defined. The article's teller example uses arrival, service-start and service-end events and queue length as state. In manufacturing, simulation helps find bottlenecks caused by excess inventory, overproduction, process variability and varying routing, and gives a whole-system view with indicators such as worker utilization, on-time delivery and scrap rate. Managers can test Lean or Six Sigma changes within the full system before committing resources. The page also gives a healthcare example where extra hours help only if the true bottleneck is solved. It does not use the term factory simulation itself, so this is the underlying modeling technique.

ontological-design.title: Ontological design is popular in design academia, but what is it? (Eye on Design)
ontological-design.notes: This article explains ontological design as the question of what design fundamentally is and does. Its core idea, summarized by Anne-Marie Willis, is that people design their world while the world acts back on them and designs them, so design shapes the conditions under which people exist and understand themselves. The concept was first formulated in the 1986 book Understanding Computers and Cognition by Terry Winograd and Fernando Flores, drawing on Humberto Maturana and Martin Heidegger, with the claim that in designing tools we are designing ways of being. Later contributors include Willis, Tony Fry (design that sustains or diminishes futures) and Arturo Escobar. Key claims are that design structures what is possible, often unnoticed; that unintended consequences are central rather than incidental; that we are inside the loop before we become aware of it, which makes alternatives seem unrealistic; and that narrow problem-solving should give way to asking what worlds design creates. It also questions celebrating individual iconic designers and examines branding. The article admits the perspective is abstract and hard to apply in practice.

golden-ticket-attack.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket, T1558.001 (MITRE ATT&CK)
golden-ticket-attack.notes: MITRE ATT&CK describes Golden Ticket as a credential access sub-technique of stealing or forging Kerberos tickets on Windows. An adversary who holds the password hash of the KRBTGT account, the service account of the key distribution center that encrypts and signs all Kerberos tickets in the domain, can forge ticket-granting tickets that yield authentication material for any account in Active Directory. The forged ticket still has to be presented to the KDC to obtain service tickets for specific resources. The hash is typically obtained through OS credential dumping, which requires privileged access to a domain controller. Tools and groups listed as having forged golden tickets include Empire, Mimikatz, Rubeus, Sliver and the Ke3chang group. To contain a golden ticket the page recommends resetting the KRBTGT password twice with replication between the resets, and rotating it roughly every 180 days, plus limiting domain admin rights to domain controllers and a small set of servers. Detection looks for abnormal ticket lifetimes, unexpected encryption types such as RC4 in modern domains, malformed logon fields and service ticket requests without a preceding ticket-granting ticket request.

commoditization.title: Commoditization (Wikipedia)
commoditization.notes: Commoditization is the process by which goods that were once distinguished by uniqueness or brand come to be seen by the market as simple commodities. Products that used to be differentiated become similar from the buyer's perspective, so competition shifts from differentiated qualities to price, and the market moves from monopolistic competition toward perfect competition. Once items look alike buyers tend to choose the cheapest one, which weakens the pricing power of manufacturers and brand owners and can erode brand value. The article separates commoditization, where proprietary things become generic, from commodification, where non-saleable things become saleable, though the social sciences sometimes use the words interchangeably. It can be a deliberate aim of a market participant or an unintended result; the example given for the latter is a trademark becoming generic. Consumers can benefit because perfect competition usually lowers prices, while branded producers often lose out. The page warns about false commoditization, where premium products with real value, especially in health, safety and security, are treated as interchangeable, creating significant risk.

golden-path.title: How We Use Golden Paths to Solve Fragmentation in Our Software Ecosystem (Spotify Engineering)
golden-path.notes: This Spotify Engineering article defines a Golden Path as the opinionated and supported way to build something, such as a backend service, website or data pipeline, with a step-by-step tutorial that walks engineers along it. Spotify created them because autonomous teams had produced a fragmented tooling landscape in which engineers learned by asking colleagues, which the author calls rumour-driven development. The goal is to make recommended tools easy to find and the route through them clear, not to restrict engineers; those who leave the path can still do so but without the same support. The first tutorial, for backend engineering, began as a Hack Week project by eight engineers in the platform organization, and tutorials now exist per discipline including data engineering, machine learning, web and audio. They are written with TechDocs and shown in the Backstage developer portal, are part of onboarding, usually completed by new engineers in their first two weeks, and are described as Spotify's most read technical documentation. The article also outlines a proposed Golden State of checks that show whether a system follows the path.

main-account.title: Main account types (Microsoft Learn, Dynamics 365 Finance)
main-account.notes: In Dynamics 365 Finance a main account is a record in the chart of accounts, and its main account type, chosen when the account is created, determines how it is used. The page lists the types: profit and loss, revenue and expense accounts are posting accounts that record revenue and expenses, and their sum determines the year-end result; balance sheet, asset, liability and equity accounts are transaction accounts that record what a legal entity owns or owes; total accounts aggregate account intervals and show the total of group balances; and a reporting type is used only for financial statement reporting in Brazil. After selecting the total type, you open the Totals option on the General tab to define the account intervals it adds up. Total accounts cannot be suspended, so the page suggests using the Active from and Active to dates to simulate suspension. The page links to a further article on setting up main account categories. It is a reference on account types rather than a full tutorial, and it does not describe the example accounts such as cash or rent expense.

multi-access-edge-computing.title: Multi-access edge computing (Wikipedia)
multi-access-edge-computing.notes: Multi-access edge computing, formerly mobile edge computing, is a network architecture concept defined by ETSI that brings cloud computing and an IT service environment to the edge of cellular networks and, more generally, of any network. Running applications and processing closer to users reduces network congestion and improves application performance. MEC is designed to run at cellular base stations or other edge nodes, letting operators deploy new services quickly and open their radio access network to authorized third parties such as developers and content providers. ETSI created an Industry Specification Group for it in 2014. The central component is a MEC application server integrated with the RAN, offering compute, storage, connectivity and real-time RAN information in a multitenant hosting environment where applications arrive as VM images or containers. Listed benefits are lower latency, reduced core signaling load and lower hosting cost. Use cases include computational offloading, content delivery and caching, mobile big data analytics, connected cars, smart venues, healthcare, smart grids and indoor positioning. The article notes that few applications had adopted MEC at the time and names AWS Wavelength as the first larger-scale commercial MEC product.

monthly-active-users.title: Active users (Wikipedia, covers monthly active users)
monthly-active-users.notes: Active users is a software performance metric that counts unique users who interact with a product within a set period, reported as daily, weekly or monthly active users or peak concurrent users. Companies compute it from their own data using actions they treat as activity, such as logging in, visiting a home page, commenting or uploading content, and methods vary and are often undisclosed. Typical uses are in social networks, games, mobile apps and online banking, in research on churn prediction, and for investors and advertisers. The ratio of daily to monthly active users is a rough engagement measure; the article cites a ratio of 0.15 as a growth tipping point and sustained values of 0.2 and above as a sign of lasting success. Criticisms include the lack of a standard definition, which makes cross-company comparison unreliable, inflated counts from simple actions, duplicate or fake accounts, weak regulation, and little insight into loyalty or behavior before and after adoption. Growth in active users does not always follow revenue, and using such data raises consent and privacy questions.

mixture-of-experts.title: Mixture of experts (Wikipedia)
mixture-of-experts.notes: Mixture of experts is a machine learning technique in which several expert networks divide a problem space into regions, a form of ensemble learning once called committee machines. A gating function takes the input and produces weights, the experts each produce outputs, and the final result is usually a weighted sum; experts and gate are trained jointly. In deep learning the motivation is conditional computation: sparsely-gated MoE, introduced by Shazeer and colleagues at Google Brain in 2017, keeps only the top-k gate values, with k typically 1 or 2, so only some experts run per input. MoE layers usually replace feedforward layers in Transformer blocks. Notable models include Switch Transformer with top-1 routing, GLaM with 1.2 trillion parameters, Mixtral 8x7B with 46.7B parameters and 8 experts, and DBRX with 132B parameters and 16 experts. The article discusses load balancing, with auxiliary losses or DeepSeek-style bias adjustments, capacity factors, token dropping, shared versus routed experts and sparse upcycling of dense models. Limits include load imbalance, discrete routing that is harder to optimize, many interacting design choices and training stability.

enterprise-content-management.title: Enterprise content management (Wikipedia)
enterprise-content-management.notes: Enterprise content management extends content management by tracking each item over its life and possibly enforcing processes for creation, approval and distribution. It provides a secure repository for analog or digital content and methods to import and present it, and it is aware of the processes of the enterprise it serves. It covers document and web content management, search, collaboration, records management, digital asset management, workflow and capture, delivered on premises, as SaaS or hybrid. AIIM defines five components: capture, manage, store, preserve and deliver. The market emerged from document management systems of the late 1980s and early 1990s, consolidated through acquisitions such as EMC buying Documentum and IBM buying FileNet, and saw Microsoft SharePoint and Oracle enter the low-cost segment from 2006. Benefits cited are efficiency, control, lower cost and faster access; ECM can support compliance with rules such as HIPAA, Sarbanes-Oxley and PCI DSS through role-based security and audit trails. In 2017 AIIM proposed the label intelligent information management. The page carries citation warnings and uses dated market figures.

cross-cutting-concerns.title: Cross-cutting concern (Wikipedia)
cross-cutting-concerns.notes: In aspect-oriented software development, a cross-cutting concern is an aspect of a program that affects several modules and cannot be contained in any one of them. Such concerns often cannot be separated cleanly from the rest of the system in design or implementation and cause scattering, where the same code is duplicated in many places, tangling, where components become heavily interdependent, or both. Procedural, functional and object-oriented styles offer no direct way to handle a primary goal together with a cross-cutting concern, so modularity suffers. The article's example is a medical records application where indexing records is core, while logging changes and authentication cut across many parts. Listed examples include logging, monitoring, caching, validation, persistence, transaction processing, synchronization, security and privacy, error handling, internationalization and memory management. Aspect-oriented programming addresses them by encapsulating each concern in an aspect, which keeps the code isolated, reusable and easier to maintain. The page cites the 1997 Kiczales paper on aspect-oriented programming and AspectJ as foundations, and gives no specific implementation mechanisms such as middleware or decorators.

shure.title: Shure (Wikipedia)
shure.notes: Shure Inc. is a private American company that designs and manufactures consumer and professional audio equipment, headquartered in Niles, Illinois, with Christine Schyvinck as CEO since 2016. Sidney N. Shure founded it in Chicago on 25 April 1925 as The Shure Radio Company, selling radio parts kits, and it later became Shure Brothers Company. Its early microphones include the Model 55 Unidyne of 1939, and during World War II it supplied microphones to the US armed forces. The SM57 (1965) and SM58 (1966) are described as the best-selling microphones in the world since the late 1960s. Other lines include Beta and KSM microphones, wireless systems such as ULX, SLX and Axient, in-ear monitors, headphones and mixers. For conferencing and installed audio it offers Microflex microphones, Microflex Advance (MXA) array microphones introduced in 2016, IntelliMix processors and room kits, and the MXA902 ceiling array from 2023. The company also made phonograph cartridges until it stopped all phono products in 2018. Manufacturing sites include Mexico and China. The article does not mention Microsoft Teams Rooms certification.

spec-kit.title: github/spec-kit (GitHub repository)
spec-kit.notes: Spec Kit is an open-source, MIT-licensed toolkit from GitHub that gives AI coding agents structured processes, reusable templates and documented outcomes, with Spec-Driven Development as its core process. In that process you set up a constitution once per project to state guiding principles such as code quality, testing and maintainability, then for each feature run commands in the agent chat: specify to describe what to build, plan to set the technical approach, tasks to break the plan into work items, and implement and converge to build and check the code until convergence is reported. Optional steps cover clarification, checklists and consistency analysis. Bundled extensions add bug fixing, which ends in a verified, partial or failed verdict, and idea assessment, which ends in go, needs-clarification or kill. Custom processes can be assembled from integrations, extensions, presets, workflows and bundles, and community catalogs can be searched, with a warning that listings are not audits or endorsements. Requirements are Python 3.11 or newer, uv and a supported AI coding agent on Linux, macOS or Windows; offline and air-gapped use and private catalogs are supported.

chain-of-thought-reasoning.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models (arXiv)
chain-of-thought-reasoning.notes: This paper, whose abstract is the page fetched, defines a chain of thought as a series of intermediate reasoning steps. Chain-of-thought prompting is a simple method in which a few worked examples that show this step-by-step reasoning are given to a large language model in the prompt. The authors argue that the ability to reason this way emerges naturally in sufficiently large language models, and that the method needs no extra training. Experiments on three large language models showed improved performance across arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning tasks. The most striking result reported is that a 540-billion-parameter model prompted with just eight chain-of-thought examples reached state-of-the-art accuracy on the GSM8K benchmark of math word problems, surpassing a fine-tuned GPT-3 model combined with a verifier. The abstract does not give detailed experimental numbers or name the other two models. As an authoritative source it establishes the technique of prompting a model to write out intermediate steps before the final answer, the idea behind later reasoning-focused models, while the page itself contains only the abstract and metadata.

adkar-model.title: ADKAR (Wikipedia)
adkar-model.notes: ADKAR is a model of individual change built from five sequential building blocks: awareness of why change is needed, desire to take part in and support it, knowledge of what to do during and after the change, ability to carry it out as required, and reinforcement to keep the results in place. Jeff Hiatt developed it and first published it in 1999 in a white paper called The Perfect Change, and later work from 2006 is associated with his organization Prosci. The model is prescriptive and goal-oriented: each milestone must be achieved to count as success, and individuals are scored from 1 to 5 on each one. A score of 3 or below is called a barrier point that must be addressed before moving on. Hiatt held that the steps run in order, begin from each person's current level and cannot be skipped or reordered. The article treats the strict sequencing as a design feature and does not describe criticism aimed specifically at ADKAR; the criticism it mentions concerns Kurt Lewin's three-step model, which some scholars called simplistic.

industrial-data-model.title: ISA-95 (Wikipedia)
industrial-data-model.notes: ISA-95, also standardized as ANSI/ISA-95 and IEC 62264, is an international standard from the International Society of Automation for building an automated interface between enterprise systems and control systems. It applies to batch, continuous and repetitive processes in any industry. Its objectives are consistent terminology, consistent information models and consistent operations models, so suppliers and manufacturers share a common foundation. Part 1 sets terminology and object models that determine which information should be exchanged and helps define the boundary between enterprise and control systems; Part 2 defines attributes for every object in Part 1, which can underpin information exchange and relational databases; Part 3 models manufacturing operations management at level 3, the production or MES layer; later parts address object models for operations management, business-to-manufacturing transactions, messaging and information exchange profiles. Part 1 includes the Purdue-style scheduling and control hierarchy, the equipment hierarchy, a functional data flow model and object models with relationships and attributes. The page does not use the phrase industrial data model; it is a standards-based example.

social-capital.title: Social capital (Wikipedia)
social-capital.notes: Social capital refers to networks of relationships that help individuals and groups reach their goals, resting on trust, shared norms and values, cooperation and reciprocity. It is studied in sociology and economics, though scholars disagree on exactly what it is. Lyda Hanifan's 1916 writing on rural schools is often cited as the earliest use of the term, and Pierre Bourdieu, James Coleman and Robert Putnam shaped the modern concept; interest grew in the late 1990s, including a World Bank research program. Common distinctions are bonding ties within similar groups, bridging ties across groups and linking ties to officials or leaders. Putnam treats it as a community resource supporting civic engagement and argues it has declined in the United States, Bourdieu sees it as a tool that helps the powerful keep advantages, and Coleman as a neutral resource that supports action. There is no consensus on measurement; methods include name generators, trust surveys and tracking participation in voluntary groups. Criticisms cover a vague definition, a questionable analogy to financial capital, possible negative effects such as exclusion, neglect of structural factors and mixed evidence about internet effects.

model-card.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting (arXiv)
model-card.notes: This paper proposes model cards: short documents that accompany a trained machine learning model and report its performance. The authors argue that released models should come with such documentation so that people can see what the models are good for and where they fall short. A model card is a brief, standardized report presenting benchmarked evaluation results under varied conditions, including performance across demographic, cultural and phenotypic groups such as race, geographic location, sex and Fitzpatrick skin type, and across intersectional groups like age combined with race. It also records the intended use context, details of how the evaluation was run and other relevant information. The purpose is transparency: clear documentation clarifies intended uses and discourages deployment in contexts where a model is poorly suited, which the authors frame as a step toward responsible democratization of machine learning and AI. The paper concentrates on human-centered models in computer vision and natural language processing but says the framework can document any trained model, and it supplies two sample cards, one for a smiling-face detector and one for a toxic-comment detector. Its focus is fairness reporting rather than governance reviews.

industrial-dmz.title: What is an Industrial DMZ? (Software Toolbox)
industrial-dmz.notes: This explainer describes an industrial DMZ as a dedicated network zone between the operational technology network and the enterprise IT network, adapted from the IT DMZ idea. Its core rule is that no traffic crosses the IT and OT boundary without terminating in the DMZ first, and it sits at Level 3.5 of the Purdue model as a third zone with its own security policy and servers. Two firewalls in series, ideally from different vendors, guard the enterprise side and the plant side, enterprise systems never connect directly to controllers, and OT should initiate outbound connections instead of accepting inbound ones. Typical occupants are read-only historian replicas, remote access jump servers with multi-factor authentication, OPC tunneling endpoints, MQTT brokers, staged patch servers and passive monitoring dashboards. Data can flow through explicit inspected port openings, outbound-only tunnels, a broker or a hardware data diode. The page cites NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, ISA/IEC 62443 and CISA guidance and warns against leftover temporary firewall rules, dual-homed workstations, using the zone as a file server or allowing internet access. The publisher sells related products, so its product claims were left out.

harvest-now-decrypt-later.title: Harvest now, decrypt later (Wikipedia)
harvest-now-decrypt-later.notes: Harvest now, decrypt later is a surveillance strategy in which an actor collects encrypted data today, although it cannot currently be read, and stores it long term in the hope of decrypting it once advances in computing or cryptanalysis allow. The hypothetical date is called Y2Q or Q-Day, in analogy to Y2K, and other names include store now, decrypt later and retrospective decryption. The usual concern is that quantum computers could eventually break current strong encryption algorithms, but any capable attack would suffice. The strategy matters most for data with a long confidentiality lifetime, such as diplomatic communications, health records, critical infrastructure logs and intellectual property. No practical quantum attacks exist yet, but data encrypted today may stay sensitive for decades. The primary defense is post-quantum cryptography, though the article notes it protects the payload and not the transmission, so traffic can still be captured. A complementary idea is physical layer or optical security that hides the signal so it cannot be recorded; those claims rest on a vendor and conference papers without independent verification. The page mentions a US roadmap proposed in 2022 for migrating to quantum-resistant algorithms.

works-council.title: Works council (Wikipedia)
works-council.notes: A works council is a shop-floor body that represents workers at firm or plant level, complementing trade unions and in some countries operating independently of them. Names vary, for example Betriebsrat in Germany and Austria, Ondernemingsraad in the Netherlands and Comité Social et Economique in France. In Germany members are elected by the workforce for four-year terms, union membership is not required and councils can exist where neither side is organized. They have two functions: co-determination, including electing board members, and participation, meaning management must consult them on specific issues and they may make proposals. They cannot call strikes or negotiate wage increases, and obstructing a works council is a criminal offence. The article traces the German history from 19th-century workers' committees through the 1920 Works Council Act, the 1952 Works Constitution Act, the 1972 revision and 2001 reforms. At EU level, European Works Councils arise from Directive 94/45/EC for companies with at least 1,000 employees and 150 in each of two countries; the 2009 recast followed. Reported effects in Germany include higher wages and productivity, with lower profitability and less benefit in small firms.

mai-1.title: Microsoft's Two New AI Models Rival OpenAI's Similar Options (eWeek)
mai-1.notes: This news article covers Microsoft's announcement of MAI-1-preview, described as its first proprietary foundation model that directly competes with partner OpenAI. According to the article it is a mixture-of-experts model designed as a generalist for everyday prompts, trained in-house on about 15,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. It handles general-purpose text tasks and is aimed mainly at consumers rather than enterprises. At launch it was in public testing on the LMArena community evaluation forum, and testers could apply for early API access. Microsoft said it would begin collecting user feedback on certain text-generation uses of the model inside Copilot within weeks. The announcement also included a voice model, MAI-Voice-1, and a separate Wikipedia article on Microsoft AI confirms that both were announced on 28 August 2025 as among the first in-house models, after products had relied mainly on OpenAI's models. The source is a technology news outlet, not a Microsoft page, and it does not describe the deep multi-step reasoning focus or a later cloud-hosted offering mentioned in the glossary entry, so only the preview model is documented here.

data-gravity.title: Data gravity (TechTarget WhatIs)
data-gravity.notes: Data gravity is described as the ability of a body of data to attract applications, services and other data, much as mass attracts objects in physics; data lakes and data warehouses are given as prime examples. IT expert Dave McCrory coined the term in 2010, and later distinguished natural data gravity, which arises as data moves to the cloud, from artificial gravity caused by outside forces such as legislation, throttling or manipulative pricing. In 2020 he released the Data Gravity Index, which measures the effect for large enterprises by metro area and industry. Gravity scales with data volume: moving large data sets is costly and slow, so applications and services tend to be placed near the data they use. Implications include higher latency when applications sit far from their data, cloud egress fees that can make migration uneconomical, extra work for every dependent application during a migration, and new gravity created by AI, machine learning and edge sources. Suggested responses include co-locating applications and data, strong governance and standards, integrating sources into a unified store, planning migrations for the eventual data size and filtering or analyzing data at the edge.

concept-drift.title: Concept drift (Wikipedia)
concept-drift.notes: Concept drift is a change in data over time that makes a model less valid: the statistical properties of the target variable, or of the input data, change in unforeseen ways, so predictions become less accurate. In machine learning it arises when the data's distribution deviates from the training data, for example when shopping behavior shifts and a sales forecast degrades. Drift is unavoidable for processes driven by human activity, so models need periodic retraining, and adding context such as season can slow but not stop the decline. Detection works by monitoring model error or the data distribution, with named methods DDM, EDDM, ADWIN and KSWIN that use error rates or sliding windows. Handling strategies are reactive, retraining after a trigger, or tracking, continually updating through online learning, frequent retraining or ensembles. The article also covers drift in software and databases, including infrastructure, structural and semantic drift, and the security setting where malware, spam and fraud classifiers degrade as adversaries change tactics, distinguishing drift from concept evolution when a wholly new class appears. It recommends time-aware evaluation to avoid leaking future information.

personal-branding.title: Personal branding (Wikipedia)
personal-branding.notes: Personal branding is a strategic effort to create, position and maintain a favorable public perception of oneself, built on individual traits and a differentiated narrative aimed at a target audience. It draws on marketing theory and on self-presentation theory about identity, reputation and image. McNally and Speak defined a personal brand in 2003 as a perception or emotion maintained by somebody other than you. Tom Peters is credited with coining the term through his 1997 article The Brand Called You, followed by The Brand You 50 in 1999, and the internet and social media made the practice accessible. Recommended practices include defining an audience and specialization, creating original content, publishing across several channels, keeping a consistent image, staying authentic and responsive, building a complete professional profile and using a visual identity. Employers increasingly screen applicants' online histories, and platforms such as LinkedIn serve as professional profiles. Critics argue that it commodifies the self, can turn artificial because platform logic shapes presentation, and pressures people to conform, while supporters say it helps people stand out. The article carries maintenance notices and some uncited claims.

migration-factory.title: The Cloud Migration Factory workflow (AWS Prescriptive Guidance)
migration-factory.notes: This AWS Prescriptive Guidance page describes the predefined workflow of Cloud Migration Factory, a solution for automating large-scale server migrations to AWS. The process has three phases. In pre-migration the team prepares the implementation environment by deploying the factory, building a migration execution server and setting up AWS application migration tooling. In migration implementation, predefined tasks automate the work: verifying prerequisites, pushing the replication agent to the source machines of a wave, checking replication status, launching servers for boot-up testing and scheduling a window for application cutover. Post-migration tasks depend on the scenario and may include removing servers from the source configuration database, decommissioning source machines and tuning performance on target EC2 instances. Migrations are organized into waves, each a group of applications and servers sharing the same cutover date. The example schedule is a three-week cycle with a build stage in week one, validation and boot-up testing in week two and cutover in week three, and all waves run in parallel so several groups can be in different stages at once. The page covers one vendor's implementation, not the generic term.

workflows-agent.title: Get started with Workflows in Microsoft 365 Copilot (Microsoft Support)
workflows-agent.notes: Workflows is an agent in Microsoft Copilot that automates tasks across Microsoft 365: you describe what you want in natural language and it generates a working workflow from supported Microsoft 365 services without code. It can automate actions in Outlook, SharePoint, Teams and Planner, run on a schedule or in response to events, collect user input with adaptive cards in Teams and use data such as calendar, tasks or lists. The agent finds services from names in the prompt, connects with your Microsoft 365 account, and lets you test the workflow, review run history and errors on an Activity page and turn it on or off or delete it. At the time of the page it was in the experimental Frontier early access program, rolling out first in the United States in English to select Microsoft 365 personal and premium plans, and admins control availability under Copilot settings for agents. Requirements include a Power Platform data loss prevention policy that allows the needed connectors. Limitations are that workflows cannot be shared, only a limited set of Microsoft connectors is supported, errors in existing workflows are not fixed automatically, and ambiguous site or channel names may be mismatched. Power Automate is the pointer for advanced needs.

infinite-capacity-planning.title: Finite capacity planning and scheduling (Microsoft Learn)
infinite-capacity-planning.notes: This Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management article explains finite capacity planning mainly by contrasting it with infinite loading. Infinite loading is not formally defined, but its example shows that work is loaded onto resources regardless of whether spare capacity exists, so resources can be overbooked, the schedule is less realistic and delivery dates are not pushed out because of capacity. Finite capacity instead considers resource limits within a configurable time fence: planned production orders are backward-scheduled from the requirement date, and if capacity is unavailable the job is scheduled when capacity exists, which can push the delivery date out; the system may also request components earlier. Outside the time fence, scheduling behaves as infinite. Finite capacity must be enabled in master planning parameters, in the master plan and on each resource. The page walks through three examples with welding and assembling operations that show how a new sales order lands under infinite loading, a one-day fence and a two-day fence. Cautions are that finite scheduling considers only reserved capacity, is not suited to capacity that changes with requirements, and that a one-day fence is probably too short for most manufacturers.

scavenger-hunt.title: Scavenger hunt (Wikipedia)
scavenger-hunt.notes: A scavenger hunt is a game in which organizers prepare a list of specific items and participants, usually in small teams, try to find or complete everything on it, typically without buying anything. The winner is either the first team to finish the list or the one that finds the most items, and variants may require photographing items or completing creative tasks. Treasure hunt is another name, though it more often involves a chain of clues leading to a single prize. Elsa Maxwell popularized the party game in the United States in the early 1930s, and the 1936 film My Man Godfrey satirized the craze. Notable events include the University of Chicago Scavenger Hunt, founded in 1987, a London event in 2012 with 466 people, and a South Korean hunt in 2023 with 3,040 participants that holds the Guinness record for the largest scavenger hunt. The article also describes related forms: Easter egg hunts, letterboxing, geocaching, armchair treasure hunts, television shows, internet hunts, video game and mobile app versions and alternate reality games. It does not describe use as a team challenge in Minecraft.

product-genealogy.title: MES traceability and genealogy (GE Vernova Software blog)
product-genealogy.notes: This vendor blog post, from a manufacturing execution software provider, defines genealogy as the complete digital record of how a product was made, linking materials, batches, equipment, operators, inspections and process data. It separates this from traceability, which follows materials and products forward and backward through production; genealogy covers the full set of relationships that produced the finished product. Records are captured automatically as work happens, so history need not be rebuilt from spreadsheets, paper or machine logs. The components named are forward traceability from received lot to customer shipment, backward traceability from finished product to suppliers and ingredient lots, lot genealogy covering consumption, splits, merges, intermediate inventory and rework, batch genealogy linking recipes, equipment and parameters to each batch, and as-built records of what actually happened, which underpin electronic batch records. The page argues that complete genealogy lets manufacturers limit recalls to affected products, supports root cause analysis and corrective action, and supports compliance topics such as 21 CFR Part 11 and GMP. Its claims about the vendor's own products are promotional and were not used here. It is not a neutral standards source.

scada.title: SCADA (Wikipedia)
scada.notes: Supervisory control and data acquisition is a control system architecture that combines computers, networked data communications and graphical user interfaces for high-level supervision of machines and processes, while sensors and actuators are monitored and controlled through programmable logic controllers or distributed control systems. The article describes levels from field devices at level 0, through I/O modules, PLCs and remote terminal units at level 1, to supervisory computers with operator screens at level 2, production control at level 3 and scheduling at level 4. Main components are supervisory computers, RTUs, PLCs, the communication infrastructure, the human-machine interface with a historian, and programmable automation controllers. Common protocols include Modbus, DNP3, Profibus and IEC 60870-5 and 61850, increasingly over TCP/IP. SCADA evolved through four generations from mainframe to web-based systems and is used in power, water, oil and gas pipelines, manufacturing and building management. Security was often overlooked in early isolated systems; opening them to office networks increased exposure, and the article cites Maroochy Shire in 2000 and Stuxnet in 2010 and recommends defense in depth, industrial firewalls, VPNs and encryption.

hire-to-retire.title: Hire to retire overview (Microsoft Learn, Dynamics 365 guidance)
hire-to-retire.notes: This Microsoft Learn guidance article describes hire to retire as an end-to-end business process covering the full employee lifecycle from planning and recruiting a workforce through onboarding, management, compensation and offboarding. It applies to Dynamics 365 Commerce, Finance, Human Resources, Project Operations and Supply Chain Management. The page lists seven component process areas: plan and recruit, onboard and manage the employee lifecycle, occupational health and safety, performance and growth, time and attendance, travel and expenses, and benefits, compensation and payroll. The flow is mostly sequential from recruiting to pay, with parallel branches after onboarding. It also maps links to other end-to-end processes: upstream inputs include forecast to plan, source to pay and project to profit, and downstream dependencies include record to report, order to cash and plan to produce, for example expenses posting to the general ledger or production time feeding payroll. Featured Dynamics 365 Human Resources capabilities include audit trails, date effectivity, benefits management, self-service, skills tracking, leave management and payroll, applicant tracking and learning integrations. The page does not discuss whether the lifecycle behaves as a network rather than a line.

kaizen.title: Kaizen (Wikipedia)
kaizen.notes: Kaizen is a Japanese word meaning improvement. Outside Japan it became a business concept holding that large gains come from the cumulative effect of many small improvements, with participation from everyone from the chief executive to assembly line workers, and it aims to eliminate waste and redundancy using existing resources. The article traces its history through W. Edwards Deming's 1947 visit to Japan and statistical quality control, the wartime Training Within Industry program in the United States and the Toyota Production System, with Masaaki Imai popularizing the term in 1986. Methods include the plan-do-check-act cycle, the five whys, 5S, the seven wastes, the three Mu of waste, unevenness and overburden, and going to the source. It names types such as point kaizen for quick individual fixes, system kaizen, line kaizen, cube kaizen across suppliers and customers, and quick or blitz kaizen. Kaizen events or blitzes focus on one issue, often for about a week. The article points to limits: point improvements in one area can cancel benefits elsewhere, events address limited scope and leave unresolved issues for later events, and the Japanese philosophy framing is described by some sources as a later interpretation.

outcome-based-pricing.title: What matters most in outsourcing: outcomes vs. tasks (CIO)
outcome-based-pricing.notes: This CIO article contrasts task-based, or input, outsourcing contracts that pay for resources such as servers, hardware or man-hours with outcome-based contracts that pay for results the business actually wants. A consultant quoted in it notes that clients generally want business results rather than infrastructure. It reports that time-and-materials contracts remain the most common model, followed by fixed price, while outcome-based contracts are at most about 15 percent of new deals and may cover only part of the work. Challenges include agreeing on outcomes when the CEO, CFO and CIO want different things, the vendor's limited control over factors such as marketing and economic conditions, the risk of gaming metrics such as customer satisfaction, and uneven results. Forrester's listed advantages are more cohesive delivery, less monitoring of individual staff, stronger incentives to innovate and potential long-term savings; drawbacks are less transparency into how work is done, limited cost visibility and extra effort for root-cause analysis. Both sides can resist: clients lose day-to-day control and need trust, while vendors absorb more risk the higher the outcome sits on the value chain. The article is dated and does not discuss build fees plus retainers or licences.

migration-cutover.title: Cutover in Storage Migration Service (Microsoft Learn)
migration-cutover.notes: This Microsoft Learn page defines cutover in the Windows Server Storage Migration Service as the phase of a migration that moves the network identity of the source computer to the destination computer. The source keeps its files but is no longer available to users and applications, while the destination takes over the source's computer name, IP addresses and Active Directory computer account so clients reach it as if it were the original server. Before cutover you provide the network configuration for the destination and may choose a new name for the source; firewall rules for SMB, Netlogon and WMI must be open on both machines. The page lists the automated steps: connecting to both computers, setting Active Directory permissions, creating temporary accounts, removing the source from the domain, renaming and re-joining it with a new identity, then renaming the destination, replacing its IP addresses and joining it under the source's original account. It also explains how to finish manually if cutover fails at a known progress stage, and notes that domain controller migration is not supported. The page covers one product's file server cutover, not the general concept of choosing a quiet weekend window.

developer-tool.title: Programming tool (Wikipedia)
developer-tool.notes: A programming tool, or software development tool, is a computer program used to develop another program, usually by helping the developer manage files. Examples of a typical workflow are a source code editor for writing source files, a compiler that turns source code into machine code, and build automation that packages programs for distribution. A toolchain is a set of tools run one after another, each passing its output to the next, and an integrated development environment combines several tools, usually an editor plus compiling, debugging and testing. The article admits that whether something counts as a development tool can be subjective: the GNU Compiler Collection exists only for development, while Notepad was not designed for programming but is often used for it. Categories include assemblers, compilers, decompilers and disassemblers; linkers, loaders and build automation; static analyzers, lint tools, code review, pretty-printers and minifiers; debuggers, memory debuggers and performance profilers; version control and bug tracking with Git and GitHub; documentation generators and GUI builders; parser generators and software development kits; and unit testing frameworks and AI-assisted tools. Valgrind is the named example of profiling and memory debugging.

kritis.title: Kritische Infrastrukturen (German Wikipedia)
kritis.notes: This German Wikipedia article defines critical infrastructure, in German KRITIS, using EU Directive 2008/114/EC: facilities, systems or parts of them that are essential for maintaining important societal functions, public health, safety and economic or social well-being, whose disruption would have significant effects. Critical refers to systemic relevance, not to a high chance of disruption. It separates technical basic infrastructure, meaning energy, water, information and communication and transport, from socio-economic infrastructure such as food, finance, emergency services and media, and points out that sectors are interdependent so failures can cascade. In Germany the BSI-KritisV regulation names seven sectors: energy, water, food, IT and telecommunications, health, finance and insurance, and transport and traffic; the civil protection office adds state and administration and media and culture, and the IT Security Act 2.0 of 2021 added a further sector. Operators must, under paragraph 8a of the BSI Act, take appropriate organizational and technical measures to protect the IT systems essential to their operation. It also covers the EU CER and NIS2 directives and companies of special public interest, sometimes called KRITIS-light.

inventory-dimensions.title: Configure inventory dimensions (Microsoft Learn training unit)
inventory-dimensions.notes: This Microsoft Learn training unit on Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management explains inventory dimensions and advises planning how inventory should work before creating them, so that dimensions reflect how the company actually categorizes and handles each item. It names three categories. Product dimensions describe the physical characteristics of an item: configuration, size, style, color and version. Storage dimensions control how items are stored and removed from inventory. Tracking dimensions are batch and serial numbers, which let companies trace products and support quality assurance and warranty handling. A packaging product dimensions feature adds three physical dimension types: storage, which is used with location volumetrics to decide how many items fit in warehouse locations and is the default; packing, used for containerization and manual packing; and nested packing, for multilevel packing, with volume calculated from depth, height, width, weight and the units entered on the released product. If a product is placed where it will not fit, the system returns an error. The version dimension tracks multiple product versions and must be enabled through a configuration key. The unit does not explain dimension groups.
